questions.question: You get an SMS: "Congratulations! You won a prize. Tap this link and enter your card details to claim it." What should you do?
choices: Tap the link to see the prize, but do not type anything
Do not tap the link. Delete the message, and do not reply
Reply to the sender and ask how to claim the prize
Tap the link and enter your details only if there is a padlock
questions.explanation: Scam messages often promise a prize and ask you to act quickly. They want your money or personal details. Do not tap links in prize messages, and do not reply. You can report suspicious messages to the CheckMate WhatsApp bot.

questions.question: A caller says he is a police officer and tells you to move your savings to a "safe account" today. What should you do?
choices: Hang up. Call the organisation yourself using its official number
Move the money as asked, then check with the police afterwards
Give him your bank details so that he can check your account is safe
Stay on the line and do exactly what he says until he is finished
questions.explanation: Real officials will not tell you to transfer money to another account. Scammers use fear and urgency to rush you. Stop talking, hang up, and check by calling the official number you look up yourself. In an emergency, call 999.

questions.question: A caller says he is from your bank and asks you to read out the OTP sent to your phone. What should you do?
choices: Read it out, because he is calling from the bank
Read out only the first three digits to prove who you are
Send it by SMS instead, so that it cannot be overheard
Never share it. Hang up and contact your bank yourself
questions.explanation: Your OTP protects your money, and nobody should ask you for it. Never give your OTP or banking information to anyone, even someone who sounds like the bank. Hang up and contact the bank using its official number or app.

questions.question: A post says: "Win a free phone! Share this post and send us your NRIC and card details." What should you do?
choices: Send only your NRIC, and keep your card details to yourself
Share the post first, then send your details to claim the prize
Ignore it. Do not share it or send any details
Send your details quickly before the prize runs out
questions.explanation: Contests that ask for a lot of personal data are a warning sign. Your NRIC and card details are what criminals use for scams and fraud. Do not share the post or give any personal information.

questions.question: A stranger messages you on WhatsApp: "I sent a 6-digit WhatsApp code to your number by mistake. Please send it to me." What should you do?
choices: Send it, then delete the chat so nobody else can see the code
Do not share the code. Scammers use it to take over your account
Send it, because the message says it was sent to you by mistake
Send it only after asking the stranger for their name
questions.explanation: Scammers ask for the 6-digit code that WhatsApp sends to you, so they can log in as you and cheat your contacts. Never share this code with anyone. Turn on two-step verification for extra protection.

questions.question: A message offers you $300 a day for a few easy online tasks, but you must first pay a "refundable" deposit. What should you do?
choices: Do not pay. High pay for little work and a deposit up front are warning signs
Pay a small part of the deposit first, to see if the job is real
Pay the deposit, because it is refundable and you will get it back later
Ask the sender for proof of the company first, then pay the deposit if it looks real
questions.explanation: Scammers dangle fast money, then ask for a deposit first. Be wary of unsolicited job offers with high pay for little effort, and do not pay to get a job. You can read more scam advice at scamalert.sg.

questions.question: You get a WhatsApp message from an unknown number: "Instant loan, no interest! Pay a small admin fee first." What should you do?
choices: Reply with your NRIC to see how much you can borrow
Pay the small admin fee, because the loan has no interest
Send your Singpass details so they can check you quickly
Ignore it, block the number and report it as spam
questions.explanation: Licensed moneylenders do not advertise loans by SMS or WhatsApp, and real lenders do not ask for a fee before the loan is released. Scammers also try to collect your NRIC and Singpass details. Block and report the number, and use only licensed moneylenders on the Ministry of Law Registry of Moneylenders.

questions.question: A friend forwards you a shocking message that says "Share with everyone now!" You have not checked if it is true. What should you do?
choices: Forward it to family only, in case the news is true
Forward it with a note saying you are not sure it is true
Do not forward it. Check it first against reliable sources
Believe it, because a friend you trust sent it to you
questions.explanation: Fake news spreads when people share before checking. Be sceptical of dramatic headlines and check with other reliable sources. You can also tell the friend who sent it that it may not be true.

questions.question: An AI chatbot gives you a confident answer about a health or money question. What is the wise thing to do?
choices: Trust it, because the answer was long and gave many details
Check important facts with a reliable source before acting
Trust it, because computers do not make mistakes
Trust it if the chatbot says it is sure and gives a reason
questions.explanation: Generative AI can state false or outdated things very confidently. This is called hallucination. Check important facts, especially about health, money or legal matters, with reliable sources, and stay in charge of the decision yourself.

questions.question: Your phone has no lock, so anyone who picks it up can open it. What is the best fix?
choices: Set a screen lock with a PIN, pattern, face or fingerprint
Keep the screen brightness low so others cannot read it
Turn the phone off every time you put it down for a while
Hide the phone icons so that nobody can find your apps
questions.explanation: A screen lock stops other people from opening your phone, apps and messages if it is lost or stolen. Choose a PIN, pattern, face or fingerprint that others cannot easily guess.

questions.question: You want a new app on your phone. Where is the safest place to download it?
choices: A link sent in an SMS, if the sender is a friend of yours
A website that offers the app for free, with no sign-in needed
A link a stranger posted in a chat group about the app
The official app store: Apple App Store or Google Play Store
questions.explanation: Fake apps can steal your data or money. Download apps only from the official app store on your phone, and uninstall apps you no longer need.

questions.question: You keep scrolling through bad news online and now feel worried and low. What should you do?
choices: Keep scrolling until you find some good news to read
Turn on more news notifications so that you stay updated
Put the phone down, take a break and talk to someone
Scroll faster so you finish all the bad news sooner
questions.explanation: Endless scrolling of bad news can raise stress and anxiety. Decide what you want to see before you go online, use a timer, and stop when you feel low. Talk to someone if it affects your mood.

questions.question: A caller says a parcel in your name was held by customs and you must pay a fine now, or you will be in trouble. What should you do?
choices: Pay the fine quickly, then ask for a receipt afterwards
Hang up. Do not pay, and check with the real organisation yourself
Press 1 to speak to an officer and ask them to prove it
Give your NRIC so they can find the parcel in their records
questions.explanation: Scammers pretend a parcel was held or that you broke a law, then demand money or personal details. Hang up, and contact the real organisation using an official number you look up yourself.

questions.question: You have chatted online for two months with someone you have never met. They suddenly ask you to send money urgently. What should you do?
choices: Do not send money. Talk to a family member or friend you trust
Send a small amount first, to test if they are honest
Send the money, because you have known them for two months
Ask for a photo of them, and send the money if it looks real
questions.explanation: Be wary of unsolicited friend requests and of urgent money requests from someone you only know online. Scammers build trust first, then ask for money. Talk to someone you trust, and read more at scamalert.sg.

questions.question: You are buying online. The seller says: "Skip the app's payment. Pay by direct bank transfer to get a discount." What should you do?
choices: Agree to the transfer, but pay only half of the price first
Pay by bank transfer, and report the seller if the item does not arrive
Pay by bank transfer, because the discount is a good deal
Say no. Pay only through the platform's own payment system
questions.explanation: A seller who asks you to bypass the platform's payment is a warning sign. Use the platform's own payment only, so the sale stays inside the platform.

questions.question: A WhatsApp group promises "guaranteed 30% profit every month, no risk". What is the safest choice?
choices: Join with a small amount first, to see if the profits are real
Join, because so many members are showing their profits
Stay away. An offer that sounds too good to be true is a warning sign
Ask the group admin whether the offer is safe, then decide
questions.explanation: Scams often use offers that are too good to be true and pressure you to act fast. Slow down, ask a trusted family member, and contact the company only through its official contact details.

questions.question: An email says: "Your account will close in 24 hours. Click here to confirm your card details." You cannot tell who sent it. What should you do?
choices: Click the link, but check that the web address starts with https
Do not click. Contact the organisation through its official website
Reply to the email and ask them to confirm it is real
Open the attachment first, to read more about the problem
questions.explanation: A message that asks you to confirm card details on a link is a phishing sign. If you cannot confirm who sent a message, do not reply or click. Contact the organisation yourself through its official website or hotline.

questions.question: Your banking app shows a request to approve a transaction that you did not make. What should you do?
choices: Tap Reject, and tell your bank if you are worried
Approve it, in case the bank is testing the app
Ignore the request and wait to see if it comes up again
Approve it, then check your account for the payment later
questions.explanation: Always check every transaction before you approve it in your banking app. If it is not yours, tap Reject. Scammers may try to get you to approve something that moves your money.

questions.question: You get an SMS that says it is from the government. How can you check that it is real?
choices: Check that the SMS uses your full name and NRIC number
Check that the link in the SMS works when you tap it
Check that the SMS says it is urgent and gives a deadline
Look at the sender name. Real government SMSes come from "gov.sg"
questions.explanation: Since 1 July 2024, government SMSes are sent under the Sender ID "gov.sg". If an SMS claims to be from the government but does not use this sender name, do not trust it.

questions.question: A news story with a dramatic headline appears on only one website, which has no About or Contact page. What should you do?
choices: Believe it, because the story is well written and full of detail
Share it with your friends first, and check whether it is true later
Be careful. Check whether other reliable sources report the same story
Trust it, because it already has so many readers and comments online
questions.explanation: Warning signs of fake news include dramatic headlines, poor spelling or grammar, no About or Contact page, and a story that appears on only one site. Check other reliable sources, or a fact-checker such as gov.sg/factually, before you believe or share it.

questions.question: An AI chatbot asks for your full name, address and bank details "to help you better". What should you do?
choices: Share your address only, and keep your bank details to yourself
Do not share them. Avoid giving AI tools personal or financial details
Share them, because chatbots keep everything you tell them private
Share them if the chatbot promises to delete them straight afterwards
questions.explanation: Do not share sensitive details such as your full name, address, phone number or financial information with AI tools. Answers about health, money or law should also be double-checked.

questions.question: You turn on two-step verification in WhatsApp. What does it add?
choices: A PIN that adds extra protection to your WhatsApp account
A list showing who has read all of your messages
A daily backup of all your chats to the cloud
A faster way to send photos and large files to others
questions.explanation: Two-step verification adds a PIN to your WhatsApp account. You turn it on in Settings, then Account, then Two-step verification. You can add a recovery email in case you forget the PIN.

questions.question: You are in a cafe with free public Wi-Fi. You need to check your bank balance. What is the better choice?
choices: Go ahead, because the cafe's Wi-Fi is free and has a password
Use the public Wi-Fi, but log out of the bank right after
Use the public Wi-Fi, but change your bank password afterwards
Wait, and use your own mobile data or a network you trust
questions.explanation: Avoid personal or confidential transactions, such as banking, on public Wi-Fi. Other people may be able to intercept what you send. Use your mobile data, or wait until you are on a network you trust.

questions.question: Which is the strongest password choice for your online accounts?
choices: A short word with a number added to it, such as Summer2024 or Lucky88
Your pet's name with your year of birth added at the end of it
A passphrase of 12 or more characters, such as five random words
One strong password that you use again for all of your accounts
questions.explanation: A strong passphrase is at least 12 characters long, for example five random words. Use a different one for each account and turn on 2FA, because reusing passwords puts every account at risk.

questions.question: An SMS says: "Your parcel could not be delivered. Pay $1.50 at this short link to reschedule." You are not expecting a parcel. What should you do?
choices: Tap the link only to read the message, and pay if it looks right
Do not tap the link. Check using the courier's official app or website
Pay the $1.50, because a small fee cannot be a scam
Reply STOP to the SMS so that they stop messaging you
questions.explanation: Scam messages ask you to take action and often use shortened or scrambled links. Do not tap short links. If you are worried, check through the official app or website of the company, which you open yourself.

questions.question: A caller says he is from a government agency. He tells you to stay on the line and pay a fine right now. What should you do?
choices: Hang up, then verify using the official hotline or website
Stay on the line and ask the caller for his name and staff ID
Stay on the line and pay, to avoid any further trouble
Pay part of the fine now, and ask for the rest to be waived
questions.explanation: Government officials never demand immediate payment, ask you to transfer money, or forbid you from hanging up. Do not panic. Hang up and verify through the official hotline, app or website, not through details the caller gives.

questions.question: You search for your bank online. The first result has a small "Sponsored" label. What is the safest way to reach your bank's site?
choices: Click the first result, because search puts the real site at the top
Click the result that has the bank's logo and name in it
Click the result that has the most reviews and stars
Type the bank's full official web address, or use its official app
questions.explanation: Sponsored results are ads, and the first result may not be the official site. For sites that handle your money or personal details, typing the full official address, or using the official app, is safer.

questions.question: A WhatsApp message from an unknown number invites you to join a paid survey panel for big pay. What should you check first?
choices: Whether the message has a professional logo and photos
Whether many other people have already joined the panel
Whether the company has a real UEN, address and phone number
Whether the sender replies to you quickly and politely
questions.explanation: Research the company and read reviews, and check that it has real credentials such as a physical address, phone number and UEN. Be careful with unsolicited invitations and big pay for little effort, and never share your PIN, password or OTP.

questions.question: You are not sure if a website can be trusted. What does "lateral reading" suggest you do?
choices: Read the same page again, more slowly and carefully
Open other reliable sources to check the website and its claims
Read the comments below the page to see what others think
Read the headline and the first line very carefully
questions.explanation: Lateral reading means leaving the page and checking what other reliable sources say about the website and its claims. It helps you judge a source instead of trusting how it looks. Fact-check sites such as gov.sg/factually can also help.

questions.question: An AI chatbot gives you website links to "prove" its answer. What should you remember?
choices: AI can invent facts and fake links, so check them yourself
Links from AI are always real, because it searches the web
A link is real if the AI sounds very sure about it
Only the first link needs to be checked, not the others
questions.explanation: AI can give inaccurate facts and links that do not exist. Check every important claim and link, and use AI to help your own thinking rather than replace it.

questions.question: You lose your phone, and it has a phone wallet with your cards. What is a good step?
choices: Wait a week in case the phone turns up before acting
Do nothing, because the phone wallet needs your face or PIN
Delete the wallet app from your new phone and carry on
Block payments remotely and tell your bank straight away
questions.explanation: Phone wallet payments are protected by your fingerprint, face or PIN, but you should still act fast if your phone is lost. Block payments remotely and contact your bank. It also helps to switch on transaction alerts from your bank.

questions.question: A caller offers to "help" with your government application and asks for your Singpass 6-digit passcode. What should you do?
choices: Share it, because the caller is helping with your application
Share only half of it, and keep the other half safe
Never share it. Your Singpass passcode is only for you
Share it if the caller can tell you your NRIC number
questions.explanation: Singpass is the official digital identity of the Singapore Government, so protect your passcode and your device. Get the Singpass app only from the official App Store or Google Play, and do not give your passcode to anyone.

questions.question: You see an app that claims to add extra features to WhatsApp. What should you do?
choices: Download it, because extra features can be useful to you
Do not download it. Use only the official WhatsApp app
Download it, but only if it has many good reviews
Download it, and delete it if it turns out to be slow
questions.explanation: Fake apps that copy WhatsApp or add extra features can look the same but risk identity fraud, data theft and malware. The real WhatsApp has built-in protection that fake apps lack.

questions.question: You get a message saying your data was in a breach, with a link to "check" it. What is the safest step?
choices: Check on the organisation's official website, not through the link
Tap the link to check whether your details were leaked
Reply with your details so the organisation can confirm them
Forward the message to your contacts to warn them first
questions.explanation: Scammers pretend to be organisations notifying you of a data breach. Check breach notices through the organisation's official website or hotline, not through the link in the message.

questions.question: A caller says he is from your internet company. He says your connection is faulty and asks you to install software so he can "fix" it. What should you do?
choices: Install it, but watch the screen closely and give him no password
Install it, because he knows which company you use for your internet
Ask him to send the link by SMS first, then install it from there
Install nothing. Hang up and call the company on its official number
questions.explanation: Tech support scams pretend to be from a telco or internet company and ask you to install software. Never install software or give remote access because a caller asks. Check by contacting the company yourself.

questions.question: You see an article headline and want to share it. You have not read the article. What should you do?
choices: Share it now, because the headline is clear enough
Share it now and read the article later when you have time
Read the whole article first, and think about who will get it
Share it if the article has many likes and comments
questions.explanation: A headline alone is not enough to judge an article. Read or watch the whole item before you share, and think about the effect on the people who will receive it.

questions.question: A caller says he is from your bank. When you doubt him, he says: "Call this number to check, it is our hotline." What should you do?
choices: Call the number he gave, because he offered it for checking
Hang up, and look up the bank's official number yourself
Call that number but give him no personal details
Ask him to call you back from a different number
questions.explanation: Verify by calling the organisation's official main number, not the number the caller gives you. A number given by the caller may lead straight back to the scammer. Stop talking if you are unsure, then check the source yourself.

questions.question: A message from a family member's account says: "I am in a hurry. Please send me money now." It feels a little unusual. What should you do?
choices: Stop, and call your family member on the number you already know
Send a small amount first, then ask when they are free
Reply and ask for their bank details before sending money
Ask them to send a photo of themselves, then send the money
questions.explanation: Hacked or spoofed accounts can pose as friends or family. Be wary of unusual requests, especially for money. Stop, and check with the person using a number you already have before you send anything.

questions.question: You get a video call from someone who looks and sounds like a relative and asks you to transfer money now. What is the safest step?
choices: Transfer the money, because you can see and hear them
Transfer a small amount first, to see if it is really them
Ask them to switch the camera on again, then transfer the money
End the call and phone your relative on a number you know
questions.explanation: Criminals can use AI to copy faces and voices, including those of loved ones. This is called a deepfake. Verify unexpected money requests by calling back on a number you already know.

questions.question: A video shows a famous person praising an investment and urging you to join now. What should you do?
choices: Join, because a famous person would not recommend a scam
Join with a small amount to test whether it works
Be careful. It could be a deepfake. Check trusted sources first
Share the video so that your friends can join in too
questions.explanation: Scammers can use AI-made videos of celebrities to promote investments. A famous face does not prove an investment is safe. Check with trusted sources, and do not rush.

questions.question: Which is a clue that a video may be a deepfake?
choices: The speaker's voice is quiet, and the whole video is only a few seconds long
Odd face movements, strange lighting, or blurring at the face edges
The video has already been shared by many people on social media
The video is posted by someone with a large number of followers
questions.explanation: Deepfake clues include unnatural facial expressions, inconsistent resolution or lighting, and blurring around the edges of the face. Check the content against other trusted sources and do not share it if you are unsure.

questions.question: An email looks like it is from a senior government leader and asks you to reply with personal details. What should you do?
choices: Do not reply. Check using reliable sources or the official website
Reply, because an email from a government leader must be genuine
Forward it to all your friends and family, to warn them about it
Reply with only your name, and keep all your other details back
questions.explanation: Fake emails pretending to be from officials have been used to get people to reply. Check against reliable sources before you respond or forward, and use scamalert.sg or the Anti-Scam hotline if you are unsure.

questions.question: Why is a digital token in your banking app safer than relying only on SMS OTPs?
choices: Tokens work without a phone or an internet connection
Tokens are free, but SMS OTPs always cost money to send
Tokens let the bank phone you to confirm each payment
Scammers can trick people into revealing SMS OTPs
questions.explanation: Phishing tricks people into giving passwords and OTPs. A digital token in your bank app is safer because scammers can trick people into revealing OTPs. Update your banking app promptly and check each transaction before you approve it.

questions.question: What does a bank feature such as POSB or DBS digiVault do?
choices: It gives you a new password each day for your banking app
It hides your account balance from anyone who sees your phone
It locks savings against scam transfers; you can unlock at an ATM
It pays you extra interest for leaving your money untouched
questions.explanation: digiVault lets you lock part or all of your savings so scammers cannot make unauthorised digital transfers from your phone. Locked money keeps earning interest, and you can unlock it at an ATM.

questions.question: On an Android phone, you want a government app. How can you tell the app is really linked to the government?
choices: Check that millions of people have downloaded the app and rated it highly
Look for the government badge next to the app's rating in Google Play
Check that the app icon looks like the official logo of a government agency
Check that the app asks you to log in with your Singpass details first
questions.explanation: Google Play shows a government badge, a building icon beside the rating, for apps it has verified as government-affiliated. Check for the badge before you install a government app, and report suspicious apps to Google Play.

questions.question: You see a QR code stuck on a lamp post that promises a free gift if you scan it. What should you do?
choices: Do not scan it. Check that a QR code is genuine before you use it
Scan it, but close the page at once if it asks for any details
Scan it, because a free gift is surely worth a quick look
Scan it, then share the link so that your friends can get a gift too
questions.explanation: QR codes can be malicious. Check that a QR code is legitimate before you scan or act on it, and be careful with unexpected or tampered-looking codes.

questions.question: Your friend chats with an AI companion app for hours every day and has stopped meeting friends. What is the healthy approach?
choices: Let the app take the place of friends, since it is always kind
Ask the app for medical advice, since it is available all day
Tell the app your bank details so that it can help you better
Use it in moderation, and keep real friends and family as the priority
questions.explanation: An AI companion imitates empathy but does not feel or understand. Use it in moderation, keep real-world relationships as the priority, and do not rely on it for medical, financial or relationship advice. Avoid giving it passwords or personal details.

questions.question: You post a photo, then delete it an hour later. What is true?
choices: It is gone for good once you press the delete button
It is deleted from the phones of everyone who saw it
It may still exist, because others may have copied or saved it
Only your friends could see it, and they cannot save it
questions.explanation: Everything you do online leaves a trail, even deleted items. Content is hard to take back and can spread beyond the people you meant to show. Think before you post, limit location sharing, and check who can see your posts.

questions.question: A friendly caller from "your telco" knows your name. He says he needs to install an app on your phone to check for problems. What should you do?
choices: Install it, because he knows your name and your telco
Say no and hang up. Never allow remote access to your phone
Install it, but watch closely what he does on the phone
Install it if he gives you a reference number to quote
questions.explanation: Knowing your name does not prove who a caller is. Never give remote access unless the representative is proven official, and do not download anything before you have verified the source.

questions.question: Concert tickets are for sale far below the usual price by a seller with no reviews who wants payment first. What is the safest choice?
choices: Do not buy. Use a platform that pays the seller only after delivery
Buy quickly, because cheap tickets like these sell out within minutes
Pay half the price now to hold them, and the other half on the day
Buy if the seller sends a clear photo of the tickets with the date
questions.explanation: A price much lower than usual, no reviews and a request to pay upfront are warning signs. Use platforms that release payment only after you receive the item, prefer meet-ups or pay on delivery, and check sellers on the CASE Company Alert List.

questions.question: Someone recommends an investment app that is not in the Apple App Store or Google Play, and says to install it from a link. What should you do?
choices: Install it, because a friend you trust recommended it to you for investing
Install it, then look at the permissions it asks for after you have started
Install it and put in only a small amount of money, to try it out first
Do not install it. Apps from outside the official stores can be malicious
questions.explanation: Scammers entice people to install malicious apps from outside the official stores, which can infect the phone and steal personal data and money. Install apps only from official app stores, and do not grant excessive or unnecessary permissions.

questions.question: A new online friend says they love you after only a week. Then they ask you urgently for money for an emergency. What is this?
choices: A sign that they trust you deeply, so it is kind to help them out
A test of trust, so send a small amount first to show that you care
A love scam warning sign. Send no money and talk to someone you trust
A normal way for an online friendship to move quickly and become close
questions.explanation: In a love scam, a quick bond is followed by an urgent request for money. Be wary of unsolicited friend requests and money requests from someone you only know online. Do not send money, and talk to a family member or friend you trust.

questions.question: An old article about a medicine is being shared as if it is new. Which check helps you most?
choices: Popularity: how many people have shared it
Currency: is the information still up to date?
Design: how professional the page looks
Length: whether the article is long and detailed
questions.explanation: Judge online information by its accuracy (is it correct), authority (who is behind it) and currency (is it up to date). Old information shared as new can mislead you, so check the date and look at other sources.

questions.question: The S.U.R.E. steps help you check information, including what AI tells you. What does the "R" stand for?
choices: Research: check other trusted sources
Report: tell the police about what you saw
Repeat: read the message again to be sure
React: reply to the sender and ask them
questions.explanation: S.U.R.E. stands for Source, Understand, Research and Evaluate. Use the steps on what you see online and on what AI tells you, and verify through trusted sources.

questions.question: Singpass now has extra safeguards, such as extra face verification checks. What should you still do?
choices: Relax, because the new checks mean scams can no longer work
Share your passcode with family, so they can help you
Write your passcode on a note kept inside your phone case
Stay alert, as scams keep changing, and protect your Singpass
questions.explanation: Safeguards help, but scams evolve, and everyone has a part to play in protecting their Singpass. Stay alert and never share your passcode.

questions.question: Someone keeps sending you threatening messages online. What is a sensible first step?
choices: Reply firmly to tell them to stop, then block them if they carry on
Delete the messages straight away so that you do not have to see them
Take screenshots as evidence, do not reply, and report to the platform
Delete the chat and tell nobody about it, so that it does not spread
questions.explanation: It is not your fault. Do not engage, keep evidence with screenshots before it is deleted, block and report to the platform, and tell someone you trust. If there are credible threats to your safety, call the police.

questions.question: You open a page that looks like your bank's, but the web address is not your bank's real address. It asks for your NRIC and card details. What should you do?
choices: Log in, because the page looks exactly like the bank's
Close it, and go to the bank through its official app or site
Log in, but type a different password to be safe
Bookmark the page so you can come back to it later
questions.explanation: Fake government or banking sites copy the real thing to collect NRIC, passport or financial details. The look of a page is not proof. Check that the address is the authentic one, or go through the bank's official app or an address you typed yourself.

questions.question: You check your transport card app and see a payment you do not recognise. What is a good step?
choices: Review your transaction history, and block the card payment if needed
Ignore it for now, because the amount is probably too small to matter
Wait until the end of the month to see whether it happens again
Ask someone you met online to look into the payment for you
questions.explanation: Review your transaction history regularly, and log out of payment apps when you are done. Know how to block a card payment and request a refund. If you do not recognise a payment, act early.

questions.question: An email says "Your parcel details" and has an attachment named "invoice.exe". You did not order anything. What should you do?
choices: Open it carefully to see what it is, and then delete the email
Forward it to a friend so they can check whether it is safe for you
Reply to ask the sender what the attachment is and who it is from
Do not open it. Delete the email; such attachments can be harmful
questions.explanation: Phishing emails can include suspicious attachments, such as .exe files. Do not click links or open attachments you did not expect. Delete the message and, if unsure, check with the organisation through its official website or hotline.

questions.question: A Facebook friend messages: "Sorry, I sent my OTP to your phone by mistake. Please send it to me." What should you do?
choices: Send it, because a friend would never try to trick you
Send it, and then change your password straight afterwards
Do not send it. Call your friend on a number you know to check
Send it, because they say it is urgent and they have apologised
questions.explanation: Scammers pretend to be friends and ask for an OTP "sent by mistake". Never share an OTP with anyone. Check by calling your friend on a number you already know.

questions.question: A man names his daughter as his HealthHub caregiver on 2 December 2025. He wants her to see his reports, ask for medicine refills and pay his hospital bill. What is true?
choices: She can manage appointments and bills, but his reports need a separate permission request
A new caregiver gets full access to his health records, and can also do refills and payments
A caregiver can read health records but is never allowed to make payments for him
Full record access only applies to caregivers who were appointed before 23 November 2025
questions.explanation: For caregivers appointed from 23 November 2025 onward, HealthHub gives access to the care recipient's available health records. Caregivers can also do supported actions such as managing appointments, asking for medication refills and paying healthcare bills. Caregiver access is not view-only.

questions.question: Mr Lim has a polyclinic appointment at 2:00 PM that can be pre-registered on HealthHub. Which time is inside the pre-registration window?
choices: Only 1:30 PM, because registration opens exactly 30 minutes before
questions.explanation: HealthHub's digital pre-registration window can open 30 to 90 minutes before the appointment. For a 2:00 PM appointment, 12:45 PM is 75 minutes before, so it is inside the window. 12:15 PM and 12:25 PM are too early, and it is not only 30 minutes before.

questions.question: At a government counter, an officer asks Priya to show that the Digital IC on her phone is live and not just a screenshot. What should she do?
choices: Take a new screenshot while the officer watches
Turn the phone sideways to show the full screen
Scan the officer's NRIC with the Singpass scanner
Tap Show barcode, to show that the Digital IC responds
questions.explanation: The Show barcode function helps show that the Digital IC is interactive and live, not a static screenshot. Taking another screenshot would not prove that the identity is genuine or current.

questions.question: Singpass can scan a QR code to log in to a website, share Myinfo, or sign a document. Which statement is correct?
choices: All three work the same way: scan the QR code, and no further confirmation should appear on screen
Myinfo sharing needs no consent once Singpass is unlocked, because you have already logged in
Login: scan and verify. Myinfo: see what is shared, then agree. Signing: check the reference code first
A reference code is needed for ordinary website login, but not for signing a document
questions.explanation: Singpass QR uses differ by task. Logging in requires authentication. Sharing Myinfo shows the information requested before you agree. Digital signing can require you to verify a reference code before you approve. The processes are not the same, even though a QR scan may be involved.

questions.question: In October 2026, Daniel types his friend's PayNow mobile number and sees only some letters of the name. Why?
choices: It is a PayNow fault, so he should never make this payment and should report it to his bank
Since 6 June 2026 retail names show some letters only; company names are full. Still check the payee
From June 2026 every PayNow name, including company names, is hidden from the person paying
Only NRIC transfers are masked; mobile number and QR payments still show the full name
questions.explanation: From 6 June 2026, PayNow shows only selected letters of a retail recipient's name instead of the full name. Company recipients still show their full registered name. Always check that what you see matches the person you mean to pay before you confirm.

questions.question: Mei Ling cannot turn Singpass on for AutoFill while making a passkey on her iPhone. Three other credential managers are already on. What should she do?
choices: Turn off one other credential manager, switch Singpass on under AutoFill & Passwords, and continue in the app
Delete her Singpass account and register again, so that the app lets her create a passkey
Turn off Face ID, because a Singpass passkey cannot be used together with face or fingerprint login
Create the passkey from the Singpass website on her phone, because the app cannot create one
questions.explanation: Singpass passkeys are made in the Singpass app, and Singpass must be switched on as a credential provider for AutoFill. An iPhone allows only a limited number of credential managers at once, so if all the places are taken, turn one off before turning Singpass on.

questions.question: Ravi wants to PayNow a friend by mobile number, PayNow another person by their NRIC/FIN, and pay a shop's SGQR that has a PayNow logo. What is correct?
choices: Use mobile numbers only, since PayNow cannot send money by NRIC/FIN or by scanning a QR
Use the NRIC/FIN only for government payments, and the mobile number for everyone else
Scan the shop's SGQR, then type in the shop's bank account number to finish paying
Use the mobile number, then the NRIC/FIN, then scan the SGQR in a banking or payment app
questions.explanation: PayNow can use several identifiers. Individuals receive money through a PayNow-registered mobile number or NRIC/FIN, and businesses may use a UEN. You can also pay a merchant by scanning an SGQR that supports PayNow. The sender normally does not need to type in the recipient's bank account number.

questions.question: A saved contact's number is taken over and sends Nurul a scam message. What is most accurate about ScamShield?
choices: It always filters the message, because it checks every SMS that arrives on her phone
It cannot check screenshots from WhatsApp or Telegram, so she cannot get help from the app
It does not filter saved contacts, for privacy, so she must judge it herself and can submit it
Once she reports the message in ScamShield, a police report is made for her automatically
questions.explanation: ScamShield does not automatically filter calls or SMSes from saved contacts, because that could affect privacy and genuine messages. A scam can still come from a hacked or spoofed familiar contact, so judge suspicious requests yourself and check or report them when needed. A ScamShield report is not a police report.

questions.question: Aisha's tablet has no SIM card. A friend says Wireless@SGx needs a Singapore SIM in the device. What is most accurate?
choices: Her friend is right: every device must have a Singapore SIM card inside it to connect to Wireless@SGx
No SIM is needed in the tablet, but setup needs internet and a local number that can get an SMS OTP
She needs no SIM, no mobile number and no internet: the tablet will find and join hotspots by itself
Wireless@SGx is only for Singapore citizens, who must log in with Singpass to use it
questions.explanation: A device does not need a Singapore SIM card inside it to use Wireless@SGx. A device without a local SIM can still be set up, but setup may need internet access and a local mobile number that can receive an SMS OTP.

questions.question: Mr Goh loses his registered SimplyGo card. He has never done Singpass Myinfo verification in the app. What is the right order?
choices: Select the card, tap Block Card, verify identity, choose how the value is refunded, then confirm
Delete the card in the app, wait 24 hours, and then ask Grab for a refund of the balance
Only unregistered cards can be blocked, because registered cards are already protected
SimplyGo can show his transactions but has no way to block a lost registered card
questions.explanation: For an eligible registered card, the SimplyGo app can block a lost card. If identity verification has not been done before, you may be asked to verify your identity first. Then choose how the remaining value is refunded and confirm the block.

questions.question: Linda wants (1) MRT or road alerts and nearby buses, (2) to review the payments on her transport card, (3) to book a private-hire car. Which apps, in that order?
choices: Grab, then MyTransport.SG, then SimplyGo
SimplyGo, then Grab, then MyTransport.SG
MyTransport.SG can do all three of these jobs
MyTransport.SG, then SimplyGo, then Grab
questions.explanation: The three apps do different jobs. MyTransport.SG gives bus arrivals, transport and traffic information, and alerts. SimplyGo manages your transport card and shows its transactions. Grab books and tracks private-hire rides.

questions.question: Hafiz typed his card details into a fake Grab page (X). Separately, his Grab login looks hacked, with strange activity (Y). What is the right response?
choices: X: reset the GrabPIN and nothing more. Y: cancel the physical credit card and nothing more
Uninstalling the Grab app fixes both problems, because it removes the fake page and the login
X: tell the bank and block the card. Y: use Emergency Switch, reset GrabPIN and report to Grab
Emergency Switch reverses completed credit-card payments at the bank, so it fixes both
questions.explanation: The right response depends on what was compromised. If card details went into a fake site, contact the bank or card issuer to secure the card. If the Grab account itself looks compromised, use Grab's security features, such as securing the account and resetting the GrabPIN, and report the activity. Uninstalling the app secures neither the card nor the account.

questions.question: Madam Tan has unpaid NLB charges and tries to borrow another book. What is correct?
choices: Borrowing carries on as normal until her unpaid charges go over $50, and then it stops
Borrowing can stop until she pays; NLB Mobile takes cards, Apple Pay, Google Pay and PayNow QR
She can pay only with cash or NETS, and the NLB Mobile app cannot take card payments
Charges can only be paid at the library counter, because the app cannot process payments
questions.explanation: Outstanding NLB charges can affect borrowing, and borrowing can be restored after payment. NLB offers digital ways to pay, including cards, mobile wallets and PayNow QR, so you do not have to visit a counter to settle charges.

questions.question: Farid paid $180 on Shopee by scanning the PayNow QR in his bank app. His return is approved. He says the money will surely go to ShopeePay. Is he right?
choices: No. It goes back by PayNow to the original payment method, so check the bank app he used
Yes, every Shopee refund goes into ShopeePay, whatever way the order was paid for
PayNow purchases cannot be refunded electronically, so he must collect $180 in cash
Shopee refunds PayNow purchases only as Shopee Coins, which he can use on later orders
questions.explanation: When a Shopee order paid by PayNow is refunded, the money goes back through the original PayNow payment method, not automatically into ShopeePay. Check the banking or payment app you originally used to scan and pay the PayNow QR.

questions.question: Cheryl makes a calendar event with a reminder 30 minutes before, and invites her brother. What is correct?
choices: Her 30-minute reminder is forced onto her brother's calendar and he cannot change it
Guests cannot have any reminders of their own for an event that someone else created
Adding more than one reminder turns the event into a repeating event every week
Guests get reminders from their own settings; her reminder is not shared with them
questions.explanation: A reminder set by the organiser is a personal notification setting. Guests using Google Calendar manage reminders through their own notification settings, so Cheryl's 30-minute reminder is not forced onto her invited guests.

questions.question: Kumar has a Monday to Friday 7:00 AM alarm. He is on leave Tuesday to Thursday this week only. What is best, where available in Google's Clock app?
choices: Switch the alarm off completely, which only skips the next time it would ring
Remove Tuesday to Thursday from the repeat days, then add them back after leave
Use Pause alarm for those dates, keeping the repeating alarm as it is
Snooze Monday's alarm until Friday so that it does not ring on the days in between
questions.explanation: Where available, Pause alarm suspends a repeating alarm for the dates you choose without changing its repeat schedule. That is better than deleting repeat days, or turning the alarm off and having to set it up again later.

questions.question: Siti is travelling where mobile data may not work. She expects to translate menus and common phrases. What is the best preparation?
choices: Wait until she has no internet, then open the app and download the language that she needs
Download the languages in advance, ideally on Wi-Fi; the camera can also translate signs and menus
Take a screenshot of every menu to translate later, because Translate cannot use the camera
Do nothing in advance: offline translation works for every language without any download
questions.explanation: You can download supported languages in advance for offline translation. Do it while you have internet, ideally on Wi-Fi. Google Translate can also use the phone camera to translate printed text such as signs, labels and menus.

questions.question: Jason wants his own microphone muted whenever he joins a Zoom meeting. A trainer wants everyone muted when they enter her meeting. What is correct?
choices: Jason turns on Keep my microphone muted; the trainer uses the host's mute-on-entry setting
Only the trainer can set Jason's microphone when he joins; he has no setting of his own
Jason's own setting also mutes everyone else who joins the meeting he attends
A microphone muted on entry can never be unmuted again during that meeting
questions.explanation: These are two different controls. A participant can set their own microphone to stay muted when they join meetings, while a host or administrator can set participants to enter muted. One person's own microphone setting does not control anyone else's.

questions.question: Melissa sets Privacy, then Groups, to My Contacts Except and leaves out Alex. What is correct?
choices: Alex is blocked completely and can never contact Melissa in a group or in a private chat
Alex is removed from every group that he and Melissa already share with each other
The setting can only be changed through WhatsApp Web, and not on the phone itself
Alex cannot add her to new groups directly but can send an invite link; her groups stay
questions.explanation: My Contacts Except... controls who can add you directly to new WhatsApp groups. An excluded person can still send you a private invitation link to join a group. The setting also does not remove you from groups you have already joined.

questions.question: A poster says Singapore Government Benefits Portal, Scan Here. Its QR code opens https://singapore-gov-benefits-secure.com with a padlock. Another opens https://go.gov.sg/example. Which conclusion is strongest?
choices: Both are government sites, because both addresses begin with https and show a padlock
The first must be real, because the words Singapore and gov are in the address
A padlock proves nothing. Government sites end in .gov.sg, so the first one is suspicious
QR codes cannot lead to harmful sites, so the web address does not matter at all
questions.explanation: HTTPS and a padlock only mean the connection is encrypted. They do not prove that a site belongs to the Government. Official Singapore Government websites use the .gov.sg domain, and go.gov.sg is an official government short-link service. A look-alike such as singapore-gov-benefits-secure.com should be treated with suspicion.
